question: Passage B indicates that a mineral glow can be told from a living one because the mineral glow:

options.A: spreads continuously along a single depositional band and fades along a smooth curve.
options.B: appears only in passages through which a stream has recently run.
options.C: takes some twenty minutes to come back after a shout or a torch beam has disturbed the stretch of ceiling.
options.D: is recorded by a meter as green rather than as orange.

question: According to the last paragraph, the licence weakened the rule about principal items because it:

options.A: let three noodle carts register for pitches on the same block.
options.B: made each vendor's place secure without her neighbours, so their help stopped being worth keeping.
options.C: gave the city the power to move a vendor to the thin end of the fourth block.
options.D: replaced the Wednesday board's authority over disputes with an annual fee and a numbered pitch issued by the city.

question: The gulls' departure in the first paragraph and their return in the next-to-last paragraph function in the passage primarily to:

options.A: mark the end of Ines's formal apprenticeship on the run.
options.B: suggest that the tourists' return will make the deckhands' work easier.
options.C: explain why the deck felt wider and less forgiving in November, once the tourists and the scraps they dropped were both gone.
options.D: bracket the winter and register, through Ines's changed reaction to them, what it did to her.

question: The author calls a revival a "translation" primarily in order to:

options.A: suggest that revivals are better judged by scholars of language than by designers.
options.B: concede that a revival can only be measured against the taste of its own century.
options.C: insist that something is always carried over by choice rather than transferred whole.
options.D: argue that a revival made abroad will differ from one made in the source's own country.
